newsitem.title: USA: Isuzu Trooper has no rollover defect - U.S. agency.
newsitem.headline: Isuzu Trooper has no rollover defect - U.S. agency.

text.p: The Isuzu Trooper sport utility vehicle, dogged for nearly a year by Consumer Reports' allegations that it rolls over too easily, was found to be defect-free by the U.S. government's auto safety agency.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said on Friday it denied a petition from Consumers Reports publisher Consumers Union that the agency conduct a defect investigation into the Trooper and its sister vehicle, the Acura SLX.

"The Isuzu Trooper has been vindicated. It is perhaps now the most thoroughly scrutinised and tested SUV (sport utility vehicle) sold in the United States," said American Isuzu Motor Co. Senior Vice President Terry Maloney.

Consumers Union on Aug. 20, 1996, slapped a "Not Acceptable" label on the Trooper and SLX, saying they were a danger to consumers because they "tipped up high on two wheels" in emergency manoeuvres during road tests.

At the same time, the group petitioned NHTSA to open a defect investigation into the luxury trucks. The actions and subsequent publicity have helped to slash Trooper sale by more than half for the first six months of 1997, to 4,313 units from 9,290 a year earlier.
Sales of the SLX, made by Isuzu in Japan but sold by Honda Motor Co. Ltd.'s Acura division, were off 63.2 percent to 448 for the same period.
NHTSA said it conducted its own tests of the vehicles and said it found no evidence an investigation would lead to a defect finding and recall order.
NHTSA spokesman Tim Hurd said the agency did not issue any rebuke to Consumers Union.
"The question was whether there is a defect that affected its prpoensity to roll over, and we said no, we can't see that there is a defect here," Hurd said.
But Consumers Union stood by its claims on Friday and sharply criticised NHTSA's decision.

"NHTSA's refusal to grant our petition is the latest in a disturbing record of misguided decisions, in which the federal safety agency has failed to protect consumers from rollover hazards. It is a serious setback for the nation's motorists," said R. David Pittle, Consumers Union's technical director.
The publishing group said it believes that NHTSA's own tests have a "unique and dangerous tendency to roll."

In the 1980s, Consumers Union waged a long-running campaign against the tiny Suzuki Samurai sport/utility vehicle, but never persuaded NHTSA to open an investigation into rollover allegation. Nevertheless, the negative publicity caused sales to plummet and hastened the vehicle's withdrawal from the U.S. market.

Suzuki Motor Corp. sued Consumers Union April 1996 for defamation, product disparagement and other claims after the magazine boasted in its 1996 anniversary issue of its own responsibility for the Samurai's dwindling sales.
